headline: Democrats seize Congress in midterm blowout, vow to rein in Trump
summary: Fueled by anger over Trump's policies, including the US-Iran war and rising costs, the Democratic Party secured a majority in the Senate and gained significant seats in the House, setting the stage for political deadlock.
details: Democrats vowed on Wednesday to use their resounding midterm victory to rein in President Donald Trump, setting up two years of possible deadlock in Washington. Trump, meanwhile, spent his first post-election appearance showing off his under-construction White House ballroom.

A wave of anger over Trump's policies, particularly the US-Iran war's role in pushing the cost of living higher, helped Democrats take the Senate, where they flipped seats in deeply Republican states for a majority of at least 54-44. Democrats also gained at least 30 seats in the House of Representatives.

This will be the first time that Trump, a Republican who also held the White House from 2017 to 2021, has had to contend with a Democratic-controlled Congress in both chambers. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, on track to become the first Black speaker of the House, stated the incoming majority will focus on affordability and accountability.

Jeffries emphasized, "We don't work for Donald Trump. We work for the American people. And the days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over." New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged his party to address voter concerns about rising prices, schools, and roads, stating, "It is not enough to simply win power. We must use it."

Trump, despite his party's sweeping defeat, showcased the ballroom he is building at the White House, calling it "relaxing." He briefly addressed the elections, telling reporters, "I'll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto."

Trump had cast the midterm elections as a referendum on the first half of his second four-year stint in the White House, repeatedly urging his Republican base to "pretend I'm on the ballot." However, voters in conservative strongholds swung dramatically toward Democrats. This shift was fueled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living, and anger at Trump's stewardship of the country.

Democrats achieved seismic victories, ending a decades-long losing streak in Texas by winning their first Senate seat there since 1988 and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, Democrats turned aside Trump's hand-picked Senate candidate.

With Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled, the Democrats' majority could potentially grow by another two seats to 56-44. Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump's administration, family, and allies, and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can also block Trump's nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise.

The Democratic victory is fueling questions about the longevity of the Supreme Court's two eldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, and the durability of its conservative majority. In the meantime, Republicans hold the reins and will have at least one must-pass piece of legislation ahead – a measure to fund the federal government past December – that they could use to enact conservative priorities during the so-called lame-duck period. The loss also upended Republicans' House leadership, with House Speaker Mike Johnson saying he would not continue to lead his caucus next year.

headline_marked: Tax change: [[Savings certificate tax no longer final]], may lead to refunds or extra pay
headline: Tax change: Savings certificate tax no longer final, may lead to refunds or extra pay
summary: New budget rules mean source tax on savings certificates is now an advance payment, shifting the tax burden based on individual income brackets.
details: In the current fiscal year's budget, source tax deducted from savings certificate profits has been removed from the list of final taxes. Previously, the 10% to 15% tax deducted at the source was considered the final liability, meaning no further tax was paid or refunded.

Under the new rules, this deduction is treated as an advance tax. At the end of the year, taxpayers will calculate their total income, and the tax will be adjusted according to their specific income tax slab (ranging from 10% to 30%).

Low and middle-income families who rely heavily on savings certificates may benefit. If their total taxable income is low, they can claim a refund for the excess tax deducted at the source by filing a tax return.

Conversely, those in higher tax brackets (above 10%) will face a higher tax burden. Since the source tax is no longer final, they must pay the difference based on their actual tax slab (e.g., 15% or 20%).
To receive a refund, investors must have a Tax Identification Number (TIN) and file a tax return. They will need to provide proof of the source tax deduction and a bank account number for the refund.
Tax officials will verify the claims and process the refunds into the designated bank accounts within 120 days of filing the return.
